html:
01 · The big idea

Startups don't start themselves

Startups take off because founders make them take off — not just because the product is good. Getting the engine going is a separate, manual, tiring job, and nobody else will do it.

Myth“Build a better mousetrap and they will come.”
RealitySomeone has to turn the crank.

Paul Graham, Do Things That Don't Scale (2013): like the crank on a car before electric starters, once it's going it keeps going.

Engine cold. A good engine, sitting still.

04 · Why founders skip the crank

Two forces pull the hand off the crank. One is a math error.

01
Personalityshyness · preferring code
I’d rather write code than talk to strangers.
A matter of comfort. Unpleasant to push through, but at least you know you’re choosing it.
02
MathThe dangerous one
10 users can’t be how the big ones started.
Sounds like the rational objection. It’s a factual error about how growth works.
→ Next: small numbers aren’t small
The reason that sounds most sensible, “the numbers are too small,” is the one that’s wrong.

The hand-crank · 02

Starting and running are two separate jobs

Job 1
Starting
Your arm

Hard, hands-on, unscalable effort by the founders. Manual, and it ends at a threshold.

Job 2
Running
Its own power

Growth that feeds itself once it catches. The crank is no longer needed.

Common mistake: expecting job 2 to begin by itself. Somebody has to turn the crank first.
“Once the engine was going, it would keep going, but there was a separate and laborious process to get it going.”
Each press is one turn. Stop pressing any time and watch what happens.

Fragility · before the engine catches

The “unstoppable juggernaut” was once ~30 days of legwork from stalling.

Operate it · same start, two hands
With ~30 days of in-person work, RPM climbs past the line. After that, the same knocks no longer stall it.
The point

Fragility wasn’t unique to Airbnb. Almost every startup is fragile at first: before growth catches, a short burst of manual effort decides whether it lives.

Analogy · newborn campfire

Blow on it and feed it twigs, or it goes out. Once it’s roaring, rain won’t stop it.

07 · Judging a cold engine

Ask the right question

Two measuring sticks, one small startup. Both read the same needle.

Wrong stick · reads the needle now

“Is this taking over the world yet?”

VerdictNo → quit.
Judging a larval startup by an established one’s standards — like calling a newborn useless because it can’t hold a job. Bill Gates went back to Harvard after starting Microsoft.
Right stick · projects the needle

“How big could this get if the founders did the right things?”

VerdictYes → keep cranking.
Right things done85%
Drag: the projection moves. The left verdict never does — it can’t see the future.
Same needle. Opposite verdicts.Don’t dismiss your own startup too early

09 — A warning signThe crank test

Be suspicious of any growth plan that skips the effort.

Ask of every planWho is turning the crank?
Plan A
“Launch big and the users will come.”
Crank: nobody. The launch or a partner is supposed to do the work. That's a projectile: one big push, then it falls.
✕ Suspect
Plan B
“We'll set up every early user ourselves.”
Crank: the founders. Their effort turns the engine over until it catches. That's a powered aircraft.
✓ Passes
Source

“It's not enough just to do something extraordinary initially. You have to make an extraordinary effort initially.”

Thrust vs. impulse

Powered aircraft, not projectiles

Many founders hope one big launch or one big-company partnership will send them flying. It rarely works: a startup doesn't coast on one push. It needs its own engine, running all the time.

A launch only has to produce a core group of happy users whose enthusiasm drives growth after that.

The cannonball gets one blast and falls. The plane keeps flying because its engine keeps turning.

title: A startup idea comes in pairs

html:
Compounding · users = 100 × (1+r)w

Small numbers aren't small

Growing 10% a week feels slow: 100 users become 110. Keep it up and the same 10% makes ~14,000 in a year and ~2 million in two.

Users at week 104
2,020,000
Gained this week: +180,000
Weekly growth rate10%
Week104
Like planting a single seed: it looks like nothing until the orchard is there.

11 / 12 · Small is an advantage engine hand still on the crank

Small is an advantage

Being tiny lets you give attention no big company can. That attention makes up for a buggy, unfinished product, and talking to users gets you the best feedback you'll ever have.

experience of being the user
= product + attention
Your startup's attention — try it
Like a neighborhood café owner who remembers your order: no chain can match that, however big it gets.

10 / The forms the crank takes

Five tactics, one arm on the crank

Each is a person doing by hand what the system can't do yet. Click a tactic to put its hand on the crank.
01
Recruit by handPinterest — at a design-bloggers conference
Instead of · word of mouth that isn't running yet
02
Delight obsessivelyWufoo — a handwritten thank-you note to each user
Instead of · happy users driving growth on their own
03
Start narrowFacebook — Harvard students only
Instead of · critical mass across a whole market
04
Build it yourselfPebble — first several hundred watches by hand
Instead of · a factory order (min. several hundred thousand $)
05
Be the softwareStripe — "instant" accounts set up manually
Instead of · automation that doesn't exist yet
0 of 5 hands on the crank
Engine cold
A thank-you card, a Harvard-only launch, hand-built watches — the same manual push.Source · P. Graham, "Do Things That Don't Scale"

12 / 12 · The takeaway

A startup idea comes in pairs

Not a scalar — a vector
startup idea = ( what you'll build, how you'll hand-start it )
01
The engine — the product you'll build
02
The crank — the unscalable things you'll do to get it going

Turn the crank until the engine catches. Done well, the crank isn't thrown away: the habits it built — chasing users, delighting them — keep running inside the company as it grows.

The crank isn't discarded — its habits keep running inside the company.
